\cb3 # **1\\. Introduction**\cb1 \
\
\cb3 ## **1.1** Clinical background\cb1 \
\
\cb3 Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) is a debilitating psychiatric condition characterised by persistent low mood, anhedonia, and cognitive impairment that significantly disrupts daily functioning (Harvey, 2011; Otte et al., 2016; Bains & Abdijadid, 2023). A critical neuroanatomical substrate implicated in the pathophysiology of MDD is the subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC), specifically the Brodmann Area 25 (Mayberg et al., 2005). The sgACC exhibits consistent and robust hyperactivity in patients with MDD compared to healthy individuals, and this hyperactivity is associated with heightened negative affect, rumination, and dysregulated autonomic and neuroendocrine responses (Morris et al., 2020). Crucially, successful antidepressant interventions - whether pharmacological, such as ketamine, or neurostimulatory - are associated with normalisation of sgACC hyperactivity, underscoring this region as a prime target for interventional neuromodulation (Morris et al., 2020).\cb1 \
\
\cb3 Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) is one of the most prevalent and disabling psychiatric conditions worldwide. Global burden of disease indicates that approximately 300 million people are affected by MDD (Vos et al., 2019), with a global point prevalence of approximately 5.7% in the adult population that has shown a gradual upward trend across both sexes (GBD 2019 Mental Disorders Collaborators, 2022). In Germany alone, approximately 7 million people were diagnosed with MDD in 2009, with diagnoses increasing by 26% between 2009 and 2017 (Steffen et al., 2020). This trend is attributable in part to growing public awareness and improved access to mental healthcare, in addition to any genuine increase in incidence. Beyond its individual impact, MDD imposes substantial socioeconomic costs: patients with treatment-resistant forms of the disorder incur approximately ten times higher healthcare and employer costs than treatment-responsive patients (McIntyre et al., 2023).\cb1 \
\
\cb3 Despite the availability of pharmacological and psychotherapeutic interventions, an estimated 30-40% of patients fail to achieve remission following two or more treatment trials - a condition termed treatment-resistant depression (TRD). The inadequacy of current treatments in this population marks an urgent clinical need for novel, targeted neuromodulatory approaches.\cb1 \
\
\cb3 ## **1.2 The sgACC**\cb1 \
\
\cb3 The sgACC _(Figure 1)_ occupies a pivotal position at the interface of affective, autonomic, and cognitive processing systems, and has emerged as one of the most consistently implicated regions in MDD pathophysiology (Drevets et al., 2008; Masten et al., 2011; Price & Drevets, 2012). This region is embedded within a broad and clinically relevant functional network. Resting-state fMRI studies have established strong functional connectivity between the sgACC and the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), insula, thalamus, amygdala, orbital frontal cortex (OFC), and medial prefrontal cortex (Fox et al., 2012; Kaiser et al., 2015; Liston et al., 2014). Among these connections, the sgACC - DLPFC axis is particularly clinically significant, with MDD patients consistently exhibited altered anticorrelation between these regions during rest, and its normalisation following treatment is strong;y associated with clinical response (Fox et al., 2012; Liston et al., 2014). By virtue of its dense connectivity with limbic and subcortical structures, the sgACC has been described as a "gateway" between the cognitive control and emotional networks (Mayberg, 2009), making it an attractive target for precision neuromodulation in TRD.\cb1 \
\
\cb3 ![](data:image/png;base64,)\cb1 \
\
\cb3 _Figure 1: Schematic overview of relevant anatomical inputs to sgACC based on anatomical connectivity findings (Dixon et al., 2017)_\cb1 \
\
\cb3 Neuroimaging studies have demonstrated robust and reproducible hyperactivity of the sgACC in patients with MDD compared to healthy individuals, with this hyperactivity characteristically associated with negative affect, rumination, and dysregulated autonomic and neuroendocrine function (Morris et al., 2020). Consequently, resting-state functional connectivity (FC) abnormalities in the sgACC network have been proposed as candidate biomarkers for MDD diagnosis and treatment stratification (Fox et al., 2012; Liston et al., 2014). Critically, normalization of sgACC hyperactivity has been observed following effective antidepressant interventions, including ketamine administration (Morris et al., 2020) and deep brain stimulation, underscoring the region's role as a treatment biomarker. This has important implications for evaluating novel interventions: because these functional architecture changes reflect therapeutic modulation, tracking sgACC FC can serve as an objective, neuroimaging-based index of target engagement. Importantly, this mechanistic validation can be leveraged even in healthy participant samples prior to clinical trials, bypassing the immediate need for symptomatic cohorts to confirm target engagement.\cb1 \
\
\cb3 ## **1.3** MDD treatments\cb1 \
\
\cb3 The standard care for MDD comprises three main treatment domains. Pharmacotherapy targets neurotransmitter systems including serotonergic, noradrenergic, gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), and glutamatergic pathways. Structured psychotherapies, such as cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT) and interpersonal therapy (IPT), target maladaptive cognitive and interpersonal patterns. Somatic or brain stimulation approaches, including transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), deep brain stimulation (DBS), and vagus nerve stimulation (VNS), provide direct or indirect modulation of neural circuits.\cb1 \
\
\cb3 Despite this breadth of options, an estimated 30-40% of patients fail to achieve remission following two or more treatment trials - a condition defined as treatment-resistant depression or treatment-refractory depression (TRD) (McIntyre et al., 2023). TRD represents the most clinically urgent and least well-served population in psychiatric practice. Among somatic approaches to TRD, DBS targeting the sgACC has demonstrated meaningful antidepressant effects by delivering electrical stimulation through surgically implanted electrodes, achieving focal modulation of deep limbic structures with millimetric spatial precision (Mayberg et al., 2005; Berlim et al., 2014). The intravenous infusion anaesthetic ketamine, acting on NMDA glutamate receptors, has similarly shown efficacy in normalising sgACC hyperactivity and producing antidepressant effects within hours in TRD (Serafini et al., 2014). However, both approaches have significant limitations: DBS requires craniotomy and carries surgical risk, electrode implantation under anaesthesia, and long-term device management, significantly restricts its use to severely refractory cases, while ketamine's effects are temporary and concern persist regarding its abuse potential and tolerability with repeated administration. These limitations underscore the need for novel, non-invasive interventions capable of reaching the sgACC with high spatial precision.\cb1 \
\
\cb3 Non-invasive brain stimulations (NIBS) techniques have emerged as a promising alternative to surgical and pharmacological interventions for TRD. Among these, repetitive TMS (rTMS) has received the most regulatand more recently the Stanford Accelerated Intelligent Neuromodulation Therapy (SAINT) in 2022. rTMS protocol namely intermittent Theta Burst Stimulation (iTBS) targeting the DLPFC based on each patient's sgACC functional connectivity, achieved remission rates of over 78% in a controlled trial (Cole et al., 2022), this directly implicates the sgACC-DLPFC network as a tractable therapeutic circuit, and demonstrates that connectivity-guided NIBS can produce clinically meaningful outcomes in TRD.\cb1 \
\
\cb3 However, these modalities are fundamentally constrained in their capacity to deliver focused stimulation to deep brain structures. The rapid spatial attenuation of electromagnetic fields through scalp, skull, and cortical tissue means that effective modulation is largely restricted to superficial cortical regions, typically within 2-3 cm of the scalp surface. The trade-off between depth and focality in electromagnetic stimulation is a fundamental physical limitation (Deng et al., 2013): approaches that increase stimulation depth necessarily sacrifice spatial specificity, and neither rTMS nor tDCS can reliably achieve focal and redirect neuromodulation of deep structures such as the sgACC.\cb1 \
\
\cb3 ## **1.4 Transcranial Ultrasound Stimulation**\cb1 \
\
\cb3 Transcranial Ultrasound Stimulation (TUS) has emerged as a cutting-edge neuromodulatory technique with superior spatial resolution and deep brain stimulation than electromagnetic techniques (Nandi et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2025; Legon et al., 2018). TUS provides a number of benefits, including both deep and superficial brain targeting, mult-target stimulation capabilities, neuromodulatory effects that can continue for tens of milliseconds to hours post-sonication (Algermissen et al., 2026), (Blackmore et al., 2023). In this study, we use low-intensity focused-ultrasound (LIFU) for direct neuromodulation, with distinction to high-intensity focused-ultrasound for surgical ablation (Meng et al., 2021). LIFU employs in the frequency range of approximately 250-800 kHz, delivered through a multi-element transducer array. Using principles of acoustic constructive interference, and correcting for skull-induced aberrations through beam phase and amplitude adjustment - a process computationally implemented via software such as k-Plan - the acoustic energy from multiple transducer elements can be steered to converge precisely at a specified intracranial target (Murphy et al., 2025). The result is a focal pressure field with high spatial resolution (Shi et al., 2025), (Yaakub et al., 2023) that can be directed to deep cortical and subcortical structures, including the sgACC, that are inaccessible to current electromagnetic techniques.\cb1 \
\
\cb3 The biophysical mechanisms through which TUS modulates neural activity are multifaceted and continue to be characterised. The primary proposed mechanisms include mechanical activation of mechanosensitive channels, intramembrane cavitation producing transient changes in membrane capacitance, and direct modulation of neuronal excitability through low-level acoustic radiation forces (Nandi et al., 2025; Murphy et al., 2025). The net modulatory effect - whether excitatory or inhibitory - depends on stimulation parameters including ultrasound frequency, pulse duration, pulse repetition frequency, duty cycle, and acoustic intensity (Nandi et al., 2025).\cb1 \
\
\cb3 TUS has shown promising neuromodulatory effects across a range of cortical and subcortical targets in human research. Studies targeting the DLPFC, motor cortex, and posterior cingulate cortex have demonstrated measurable changes in BOLD signal, evoked potentials, and behaviour (Wang et al., 2025). Of direct translational relevance, Riis et al. (2024) demonstrated that focused ultrasound targeting the subcallosal cingulate - a region substantially overlapping with the sgACC - produced measurable antidepressant effects in patients with TRD. More recently, a metalens-based TUS device targeting the subcallosal cingulate across five TRD patients produced an average reduction in depression severity of approximately 61% over a five-day treatment course (Attali et al., 2025). Separately, a sham-controlled fMRI study of focused TUS directly targeting the sgACC in healthy adults demonstrated post-sonication increases in sgACC whole-brain functional connectivity, with a selective redistribution toward cognitive control and salience networks - providing direct evidence that TUS can reconfigure the sgACC's large-scale network dynamics in vivo (Malave et al., 2025).\cb1 \
\
\cb3 ## **1.5 Resting-State fMRI**\cb1 \
\
\cb3 Resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) exploits spontaneous fluctuations in the blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signal to characterise the intrinsic functional architecture of the brain - specifically, the temporal correlation of BOLD signals between spatially separate brain regions during task-free conditions. These correlations, or functional connectivity (FC) measures, provide a sensitive and reliable readout of network-level neural organisation that is disrupted in MDD and modulated by effective treatment (Liston et al., 2014; Fox et al., 2012).\cb1 \
\
\cb3 In the offline TUS protocol employed in this thesis, rs-fMRI is acquired both before and after TUS delivery, with the stimulation occurring outside the scanner. This avoids electromagnetic compatibility challenges between the ultrasound transducer and MRI hardware and mitigates acoustic noise artefacts that would otherwise confound BOLD signal acquisition. FC analysis of the sgACC in the post-stimulation rs-fMRI scan allows quantification of TUS-induced changes in sgACC network dynamics relative to baseline fMRI and relative to the control condition, providing a neural measure of target engagement.\cb1 \
\
\cb3 The ability to study intrinsic network structure at rest has broader clinical significance such as resting-state connectivity abnormalities in the sgACC and its network are proposed as potential biomarkers for MDD diagnosis and treatment stratification (Fox et al., 2012; Liston et al., 2014). Establishing that TUS can modulate these network measures in a controlled, focal, and non-invasive manner in healthy participants is a prerequisite for translating this approach to clinical populations.\cb1 \
\
\cb3 ## **1.6 Aims**\cb1 \
\
\cb3 The primary aim of this thesis is to investigate the feasibility of modulating sgACC neural activity in healthy human participants using an offline focused TUS protocol, and to characterise the resulting changes in sgACC functional network connectivity using rs-fMRI. This work seeks to establish proof of neural target engagement as a foundational step toward the clinical translation of TUS for TRD. Secondary aims include characterising the temporal dynamics of TUS-induced connectivity changes across post-stimulation time points and validating the full intervention workflow incorporating personalised acoustic simulation, neuronavigation-guided transducer placement, and compliance with ITRUSST safety guidelines (Aubry et al., 2025; Murphy et al., 2025).\cb1 \
\
\cb3 The following hypotheses are investigated:\cb1 \
\
\cb3 - Hypothesis 1: TUS to the sgACC will be localized and focus, this result in network-level functional connectivity changes specific to the targeted region, compared to the defocused stimulation control condition.\cb1 \
\cb3 - Hypothesis 2: Network-level changes in sgACC functional connectivity will vary over time.\cb1 \
\
\cb3 # **2\\. Methods**\cb1 \
\
\cb3 ## **2.1 Study** d**esign**\cb1 \
\
\cb3 This study is designed as a quantitative, within-subject, sham-controlled empirical experiment to evaluate the neuromodulatory effects of offline focused TUS on sgACC functional connectivity in healthy human volunteers. Each participant undergoes two experimental sessions in counterbalanced order: an active stimulation session (focused TUS targeting the sgACC) and a control session (defocused TUS), both in left and right hemisphere. The within-subject crossover structure minimises inter-individual variance and increases statistical sensitivity for detecting TUS-induced effects. All procedures are conducted in accordance with the ethical standards of the Declaration of Helsinki and have received institutional review board approval.\cb1 \
\
\cb3 ## **2.2 Participants**\cb1 \
\
\cb3 12 healthy adult volunteers are recruited. Prior to enrolment, all participants are screened for standard MRI contraindications (ferromagnetic implants, claustrophobia, pregnancy) as well as TUS-specific contraindications, history of neurological or psychiatric disorders, use of psychoactive medication, and prior neurosurgical procedures. Participants with any contraindication to MRI or TUS are excluded. Fully signed consent form is obtained from all participants prior to enrolment.\cb1 \
\
\cb3 ## **2.3** Study design\cb1 \
\
\cb3 The study design follows this scheme: (1) a screening and structural MRI intake scan, (2) acoustic simulation, (3) two counter-balanced experimental and control sessions (focused and defocused TUS), (4) post-hoc simulation and (5) data analysis. Stimulation sessions are separated by ideally one week (3-5 days minimum) to allow for washout of any potential accumulated neuromodulatory effects.\cb1 \
\
\cb3 ### Screening and structural MRI session\cb1 \
\
\cb3 Prior to experimental sessions, each participant undergoes structural MRI on a Siemens Prisma 3T scanner (Siemens Healthineers, Erlangen, Germany) using a custom MR coil designed to accommodate the TUS transducer geometry. High-resolution T1 and PETRA image is acquired for each participant to support individualised target localisation and acoustic simulation. The sgACC target is defined on each participant's native structural image using anatomical landmarks anchored to the BA25 probabilistic atlas mask. These masks are generated via nonlinear registration (warping) of a standard-space BA25 probability map to each participant's native MRI space. Both left and right sgACC targets are identified and simulated. Bilateral stimulation is included to reduce the possibility of hemispheric compensation, consistent with evidence from stroke studies showing that the contralateral homologous region can compensate for a damaged area, and to improve the likelihood of capturing the clinically relevant neural substrate given anatomical variability between hemispheres.\cb1 \
\
\cb3 Between the screening session and the first experimental session, individualised k-Plan acoustic simulations are performed and reviewed for optimized transducer position, optimized intensity target and safety compliance (See section 2.4)\cb1 \
\
\cb3 ### Experimental sessions\cb1 \
\
\cb3 On each stimulation day, participants arrive at the laboratory and are asked for filling the MRI suitability check and screening NIBS form. TUS stimulation (focused or defocused, counterbalanced) is delivered outside the MRI scanner. Immediately following stimulation, participants are transferred to the MRI scanner for resting-state fMRI acquisition at three post-TUS time points (15, 30, and 45 minutes post-sonication), in addition to a pre-TUS baseline scan. Each resting-state scan lasts 10 minutes, separated by 5-minute rest intervals. Following each scan and TUS delivery session, participants were asked a few questions rating perceived sound level, skin sensation, and any adverse sensations experienced during TUS delivery and fMRI scan.\cb1 \
\
\cb3 ## **2.4** TUS Procedure\cb1 \
\
\cb3 ### Target localisation\cb1 \
\
\cb3 The sgACC target is defined on each participant's native structural image using anatomical landmarks anchored to the BA25 probabilistic atlas mask. Anatomically individualised BA25 masks are preferred over spherical ROI approaches, as they provide personalised and spatially accurate representations of the sgACC that account for inter-individual anatomical variability. These masks are generated via nonlinear registration (warping) of a standard-space BA25 probability map to each participant's native MRI space using FSL tools (ANTS).\cb1 \
\
\cb3 Both left and right sgACC targets are identified and simulated. Bilateral stimulation is included to reduce the possibility of hemispheric compensation - consistent with evidence from stroke literature showing that the contralateral homologous region can compensate for a damaged area - and to improve the likelihood of capturing the clinically relevant neural substrate given inter-hemispheric anatomical variability.\cb1 \
\
\cb3 ### Transducer position\cb1 \
\
\cb3 After intake structural MRI scan, we took 5 transducer positions on each side (left and right hemisphere), normally on the frontal temporal corner of the forehead. Reproducible transducer placement across sessions is achieved using the Localite optical neuronavigation system (Localite GmbH, Bonn, Germany). Prior to each stimulation session, the participant's head is co-registered to their structural MRI, enabling real-time visualisation of the actual transducer position relative to the planned position. During acoustic delivery, transducer positions are recorded through internal timing for post-hoc check.\cb1 \
\
\cb3 ### Acoustic simulation\cb1 \
\
\cb3 The primary planning image is a pseudo-CT derived from the participant's PETRA (Pointwise Encoding Time Reduction with Radial Acquisition) structural MR image, which provides enhanced bone contrast suitable for skull segmentation. This pseudo-CT is calibrated to map Hounsfield Units (HU) to mass density (kg/m\'b3), from which the speed of sound (m/s) is subsequently derived, enabling the simulation to model subject-specific skull geometry and acoustic properties. A T1-weighted image is loaded as a secondary planning image to define soft-tissue boundaries and the precise coordinates of the bilateral sgACC masks. By co-registering these multimodal images within k-Plan, the simulation accounts for the complex interactions between the ultrasound beam and the heterogeneous bone structure while ensuring the acoustic focus remains targeted on the neural region of interest. Other files are GUMMAKER files that store information on the transducer positions and sgACC masks. The simulation pipeline proceeds in three sequential optimisation steps. First, the optimal transducer position is identified by evaluating the focal quality and minimizing off-target pressure distribution across five positions; the position yielding the lowest peak skull pressure is selected, as this indicates minimal acoustic energy absorption, a higher efficiency ratio of energy delivered to the target, thereby reducing thermal risk at the cranial interface. Second, the acoustic intensity is optimised for the selected position to ensure adherence to safety limits, specifically mechanical index (MI) and thermal dose (TD). The target spatial peak pulse-average intensity (Isppa) is optimized for both the left and right hemispheres. A single unified intensity value is applied to the bilateral sgACC to maintain consistency. Third, thermal safety simulations are conducted for both the left and right sgACC plans under linked simulation conditions with a 120-second cooling time between sonications to prevent cumulative heat build-up. In the experimental (focused) condition, the transducer is positioned and phased such that constructive interference of the 256 individual element waveforms - following skull aberration and beam phase correction - produces a focal pressure field at the sgACC. In the control (defocused) condition, the phase of each transducer element is randomised, preventing the formation of a focal zone within the brain. This design ensures that the total input energy emitted from the transducer remains identical in both sessions as a blinding technique, while avoid neuromodulatory effects at the target. While this effectively eliminates neuromodulatory effects at the target, it is important to note that this approach may not ensure comparable somatosensory or auditory sensations across both conditions.\cb1 \
\
\cb3 ### TUS protocol\cb1 \
\
\cb3 Ultrasonic stimulation is delivered outside the MRI scanner through 256-element focused ultrasound phased-array transducer, operating at a centre frequency of 286 kHz. Stimulation parameters following 5Hz protocol (pulse duration (PD) 25ms including a 5ms ramp; pulse repetition interval (PRI) 200 ms; duty cycle (DC) = PD/PRI = 10%; total stimulation duration 80 seconds, yielding 400 sonication pulses per hemisphere). Spatial peak pulse-average intensity (ISPPA) target values are in the range of 2-8 W/cm\'b2. These parameters are consistent with the parameter space established for human TUS neuromodulation research (Murphy et al., 2025) and with prior work employing a 5 Hz pulsed protocol for subcortical neuromodulation (Yaakub et al., 2023; Oghli et al., 2023). The offline design is preferred to avoid electromagnetic compatibility issues between TUS equipment and MRI hardware, and to eliminate concurrent acoustic noise as a confound in BOLD signal acquisition\cb1 \
\
\cb3 ## 2.5 Data Recording\cb1 \
\
\cb3 ### MRI scanner: Siemens Prisma 3T (Siemens Healthineers, Erlangen, Germany), with a custom MR coil designed for compatibility with the TUS transducer\cb1 \
\
\cb3 ### Structural MRI\cb1 \
\
\cb3 A high-resolution T1-weighted anatomical image and a PETRA (Pointwise Encoding Time Reduction with Radial Acquisition) image are acquired at the screening session. The T1 image provides the anatomical reference for target localisation, FSL registration, and fMRI preprocessing. The PETRA image, which is less susceptible to bone-related signal dropout, provides additional information to improve skull segmentation accuracy within k-Plan acoustic simulations.\cb1 \
\
\cb3 ### Resting-state fMRI\cb1 \
\
\cb3 Resting-state fMRI data are acquired on the Siemens Prisma 3T scanner using a gradient-echo echo-planar imaging (EPI) sequence at four time points per experimental session: one pre-stimulation baseline scan, and three post-TUS scans at 15, 30, and 45 minutes following TUS delivery. Each scan lasts 10 minutes, separated by 5-minute rest intervals. During each scan, participants are instructed to remain awake and still, fixate on a central cross presented on a screen, remain in the supine position (note: the T1 structural image is also acquired in the supine position, as even 3-4 mm of head repositioning can result in off-target localisation due to brain shift), and refrain from engaging in any deliberate cognitive tasks.\cb1 \
\
\cb3 ## **2.**6 Data a**nalysis**\cb1 \
\
\cb3 FSL (FMRIB Software Library, University of Oxford) for structural image processing, ANTs, and resting-state fMRI preprocessing and functional connectivity analysis.\cb1 \
\
\cb3 ### fMRI preprocessing\cb1 \
\
\cb3 Functional MRI preprocessing is performed using fMRIPrep 24.0.1 (Esteban et al., 2019; RRID:SCR_016216), a robust and reproducible preprocessing pipeline built on Nipype 1.8.6 (Gorgolewski et al., 2011; RRID:SCR_002502). The full fMRIPrep preprocessing workflow includes the following steps.\cb1 \
\
\cb3 Anatomical preprocessing: The T1w image is corrected for intensity non-uniformity (INU) using N4BiasFieldCorrection (Tustison et al., 2010; ANTs 2.5.1). Skull-stripping is performed using the antsBrainExtraction.sh workflow (ANTs), with OASIS30ANTs as the target template. Brain tissue segmentation into grey matter (GM), white matter (WM), and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is performed using FAST (FSL 6.0.5.1; Zhang et al., 2001). Brain surfaces are reconstructed using FreeSurfer's recon-all (v7.3.2; Dale et al., 1999), with pial surface refinement aided by the co-registered T2-weighted image where available. Spatial normalisation to MNI standard space is performed via nonlinear registration with antsRegistration (ANTs 2.5.1), targeting both MNI152NLin6Asym and MNI152NLin2009cAsym templates accessed via TemplateFlow (Ciric et al., 2022).\cb1 \
\
\cb3 Functional preprocessing: For each BOLD run, a reference volume is first generated from the EPI time series. Head motion correction is performed using MCFLIRT (FSL; Jenkinson et al., 2002), estimating six rigid-body motion parameters (three rotations, three translations). Susceptibility distortion correction is applied using the B0 fieldmap acquired per session, aligned to the EPI reference with rigid registration using topup (Andersson et al., 2003; FSL 6.0.5.1). The BOLD reference is co-registered to the T1w structural image using boundary-based registration (bbregister, FreeSurfer; Greve & Fischl, 2009) with six degrees of freedom. The preprocessed BOLD time series is then resampled to MNI152NLin2009cAsym standard space using a single interpolation step composing all transformations (motion correction, distortion correction, and co-registration), with cubic B-spline interpolation.\cb1 \
\
\cb3 Confound estimation: Framewise displacement (FD) is computed following Power et al. (2014) and Jenkinson et al. (2002). Component-based noise correction (CompCor; Behzadi et al., 2007) is applied: anatomical CompCor (aCompCor) components are estimated from WM and CSF masks in anatomical space, and temporal CompCor (tCompCor) components from the top 2% most variable voxels. Components are retained until they explain 50% of variance within their respective nuisance masks. Motion parameter time series are expanded with temporal derivatives and quadratic terms (Satterthwaite et al., 2013). Frames exceeding FD > 0.5 mm or standardised DVARS > 1.5 are flagged as motion outliers and excluded from connectivity analysis. Additional noise components are estimated from a thin crown of voxels at the brain edge (Patriat et al., 2017).\cb1 \
\
\cb3 ### Functional connectivity analysis\cb1 \
\
\cb3 Seed-based functional connectivity (FC) analysis is performed using FSL (FMRIB Software Library, University of Oxford) and Nilearn 0.10.4 (Abraham et al., 2014; RRID:SCR_001362). The individualised BA25 mask (described in Section 2.4) is used as the sgACC seed region in each participant's native MRI space. The mean BOLD time series is extracted from this seed region for each participant, session, and time point, following removal of nuisance regressors (the expanded motion parameters, aCompCor components, WM and CSF signals, and motion outlier regressors). Whole-brain FC maps are computed by correlating the sgACC seed time series with the BOLD signal of every brain voxel. Fisher's r-to-z transformation is applied to all correlation coefficients prior to group-level statistical inference.\cb1 \
\
\cb3 ## **2.**8 Statistics\cb1 \
\
\cb3 To test Hypothesis 1, differences in sgACC functional connectivity between the focused and defocused TUS conditions are assessed at the group level using paired-sample t-tests, with cluster-level correction for multiple comparisons (family-wise error rate, FWE-corrected p < 0.05). This contrast isolates TUS-specific modulation of sgACC network connectivity from non-specific effects of acoustic exposure.\cb1 \
\
\cb3 To test Hypothesis 2, the temporal dynamics of TUS-induced connectivity changes are evaluated by comparing post-stimulation connectivity maps across the three time points (15, 30, and 45 minutes post-TUS) within the active TUS condition, using ... Post-hoc pairwise comparisons are conducted with appropriate correction for multiple comparisons.\cb1 \
\
\cb3 Safety parameters recorded per session are summarised descriptively. Key mechanical and thermal thresholds verified per ITRUSST guidelines (Aubry et al., 2025) are:\cb1 \
\
\cb3 \uc0\u9679  Mechanical index (MI) \u8804  1.9 (primary cavitation safety threshold)\cb1 \
\
\cb3 \uc0\u9679  Thermal dose \u8804  2 CEM43 for brain tissue (assuming baseline temperature 37\'b0C)\cb1 \
\
\cb3 \uc0\u9679  Thermal dose \u8804  16 CEM43 for bone tissue\cb1 \
\
\cb3 \uc0\u9679  Thermal dose \u8804  21 CEM43 for skin tissue\cb1 \
\
\cb3 Adverse event data from the post-session questionnaire (sound level, skin sensation, and other subjective experiences) are summarised descriptively and used to assess blinding efficacy across focused and defocused conditions.\cb1 \
\
\cb3 # 3\\. Results\cb1 \
\
\cb3 ## 3.1 Participants\cb1 \
\
\cb3 - So far, we have collected 5 participants: 3 females and 2 males. The mean age was 25.4 \'b1 4.3 years, with an age range of 21-30 years.\cb1 \
\
\cb3 ## 3.2 Acoustic Simulation Results\cb1 \
\
\cb3 - ROI visualization, Pressure map, Temperature map\cb1 \
\
\cb3 Display as coronal/axial/sagittal overlays on the T1w image. Optionally show all 5 participants' masks in MNI space to illustrate inter-individual variability.\cb1 \
\
\cb3 - Show focal zone, peak in-situ pressure and temperature at sgACC\cb1 \
\cb3 - 3dB focal volume overlapping with sgACC mask: Compute the -3dB pressure half-maximum ellipsoid from the simulation and show its overlap with the BA25 mask. Report: focal spot dimensions (axial \'d7 lateral FWHM in mm), Dice overlap coefficient or % of focal volume within BA25 mask, distance from focal centre to BA25 centroid (mm). This is the key targeting precision figure.\cb1 \
\
\cb3 \\- kplan parameters table\cb1 \
\
\cb3 ## 3.3 Post-hoc simulation\cb1 \
\
\cb3 - Summary plot of maximum displacement from the reference position. Report mean \'b1 SD of positional drift (in mm and degrees) of all Tx positions during TUS.\cb1 \
\cb3 - Histogram of Tx positions variabilities by group and explain how we choose the Tx positions to do post-hoc.\cb1 \
\cb3 - Plot actual vs planned. Tx positions, target pressure/ temperature focal zone (show overlapped pictures)\cb1 \
\
\cb3 Real-time transducer positions were recorded throughout each TUS session using a neuronavigation system (GUM marker tracking), yielding 83 position samples for the left hemisphere and 82 for the right, each encoded as a 4\'d74 rigid-body transformation matrix in RAS space (mm).\cb1 \
\
\cb3 **Clustering.** To identify the stable recording period and remove transient positional drift, we applied DBSCAN (Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise; Ester et al., 1996) to the 3D translation vectors extracted from each transformation matrix. The neighbourhood radius parameter \uc0\u949  was selected automatically per hemisphere using the 4-nearest-neighbour (4-NN) elbow method: for each recorded position, the distance to its 4th nearest neighbour was computed; these distances were sorted in ascending order and the point of maximum curvature (elbow) of the resulting curve was identified as the natural spatial scale of the point cloud. This yielded \u949  = 0.151 mm for the left hemisphere and \u949  = 0.310 mm for the right (minimum cluster size = 3 points). This data-driven approach was preferred over a fixed threshold because the total spatial spread of the recorded positions was sub-millimetre for the left hemisphere (< 1 mm across all axes) and approximately 2-3 mm for the right, making a universal \u949  inappropriate.\cb1 \
\
\cb3 **Cluster selection.** DBSCAN partitioned the left hemisphere positions into one cluster (n = 82) with one noise point, confirming highly consistent transducer placement throughout the session. For the right hemisphere, four clusters were identified (sizes: 62, 8, 5, 4) alongside three noise points. Temporal inspection of the cluster membership revealed that the three smaller clusters corresponded to the first ~20 pulses (XML indices 91-110), reflecting an initial settling period immediately after transducer placement. The largest cluster (n = 62, XML indices 111-172) represented the stable recording period and was selected as the representative epoch for both hemispheres.\cb1 \
\
\cb3 **Medoid computation.** Within the selected cluster, the representative transducer position was defined as the _medoid_ - the real observed position that minimises the sum of pairwise L1 (Manhattan) distances to all other cluster members:\cb1 \
\
\cb3 ![](data:image/png;base64,)\cb1 \
\
\cb3 where C denotes the set of positions in the selected cluster and xi \uc0\u8712  R^3 is the translation vector of the ii i-th position. The medoid was preferred over the centroid because it corresponds to an actual measured transducer pose (position and orientation), ensuring the full 4\'d74 transformation matrix submitted to post-hoc acoustic simulation in kPlan is a physically realised configuration rather than an interpolated one.\cb1 \
\
\cb3 **Result.** The selected representative positions were: left hemisphere - XML index 44 (t = 42.1 s; X = 52.823, Y = 155.099, Z = 153.215 mm); right hemisphere - XML index 142 (t = 54.9 s; X = 199.533, Y = 156.372, Z = 140.536 mm). Translational drift across all recorded positions relative to the planned reference positions (L-3 and R-5) was 1.79 \'b1 0.12 mm (left) and 2.61 \'b1 0.38 mm (right); angular drift was 1.40 \'b1 0.07\'b0 (left) and 1.38 \'b1 0.24\'b0 (right), consistent with acceptable neuronavigation tolerances reported in TUS literature.\cb1 \
\
